name: Jacobs Engineering Group Inc.
warningSignals: Defense budget appropriations cycle volatility; FY2025 continuing resolution risk
Supply-chain labor inflation in skilled trades; project margin compression in 2024
Geopolitical concentration: Middle East and Europe infrastructure exposure to regional instability
opportunitySignals: CHIPS Act and IRA funding acceleration driving semiconductor fab design/build demand
NATO expansion and European defense modernization (Poland, Baltics, Germany) infrastructure buildout
U.S. Army Corps of Engineers climate resilience and water infrastructure modernization programs

enginesRun: Defense & Security segment (40% of revenue): military base modernization, nuclear facility engineering
Critical Infrastructure segment (35% of revenue): energy, water, transportation systems
Advanced Markets segment (25% of revenue): semiconductors, life sciences, data centers
engineOutputs: FY2024 backlog: $61.2B (disclosed in Q3 2024 earnings); 2.8x revenue multiple
Organic growth target 4-6% CAGR through 2026; margin expansion via operational leverage

domainRelevance: Jacobs Engineering is the largest pure-play engineering and construction services firm serving U.S. federal defense, national security, and critical infrastructure. The company holds prime contracts across ICBM modernization, nuclear weapons complex operations, military base infrastructure, and classified intelligence facility design—making it a structural linchpin in the defense-industrial base. Its $61B backlog and 40% revenue exposure to defense/security positions it as a bellwether for Pentagon spending cycles and geopolitical risk appetite.
portalRelevance: Jacobs is a Tier-1 anchor in the defense-industrial ecosystem and a leading indicator of U.S. government capital expenditure on infrastructure and national security. Its contract wins, margin trends, and backlog conversion rates signal demand for advanced manufacturing, energy security, and military modernization—critical inputs for equity and credit models tracking defense spending, infrastructure stimulus, and supply-chain resilience. The company's exposure to both classified defense work and commercial critical infrastructure makes it a unique proxy for government policy execution.

notes.cohortStatus: Anchor peer in engineering services; comparable to Bechtel (private), Fluor, AECOM, Parsons
notes.envelopeStatus: ELIGIBLE_NOW; strong backlog visibility, stable margins, low financial distress

intelligenceCycle.name: Signal Capture
items: Quarterly backlog prints and contract award announcements (8-K filings, earnings calls)
Defense appropriations bills and continuing resolution votes (Congressional Budget Office tracking)
Margin trends by segment and project-level profitability disclosures (10-K Item 7 MD&A)
Supply-chain cost inflation indices for labor, steel, and specialty materials (supplier surveys, earnings guidance)

intelligenceCycle.name: State Estimation
items: Backlog-to-revenue ratio and conversion velocity; current 2.8x suggests 2.5-3 year revenue visibility
Free cash flow trajectory and working capital management; FY2024 FCF ~$1.8B
Debt/EBITDA leverage ratio; current ~2.1x; target <2.0x by 2026
Segment profitability mix: Defense/Security EBITDA margin ~12-13%; Critical Infrastructure ~10-11%

intelligenceCycle.name: Diagnosis
items: Pattern match: large backlog + government customer concentration = revenue visibility but margin compression risk if labor costs accelerate
Cyclical inflection risk: Pentagon budget caps or sequestration would trigger 15-20% revenue headwind within 12-18 months
Structural opportunity: CHIPS Act and IRA funding unlocking $200B+ in semiconductor and clean-energy infrastructure; Jacobs positioned to capture 8-12% of addressable market

intelligenceCycle.name: Regulation
items: Hedge defense-budget concentration via overweight to Critical Infrastructure and Advanced Markets segments (target 60% non-defense by 2027)
Monitor CFIUS and export-control changes affecting classified work and foreign JV partnerships
Track labor cost inflation via commodity indices (BLS employment cost index for construction); model 3-5% annual wage growth impact on margins

intelligenceCycle.name: Action
items: Long-term thesis: Jacobs as a play on U.S. government infrastructure and defense modernization; overweight on CHIPS Act tailwinds
Tactical: Monitor Q4 2024 backlog conversion and FY2025 margin guidance; watch for project delays or cost overruns in nuclear or military programs
Capital allocation: Expect 2-3% dividend growth and $500M-$1B annual share buybacks; monitor debt paydown progress toward 1.8x leverage target

intelligenceCycle.name: Feedback
items: Quarterly earnings: track backlog growth, segment margin trends, and free cash flow vs. guidance
8-K filings: monitor major contract wins (>$500M), project delays, or executive changes
Stock price reaction to defense appropriations votes and Pentagon budget announcements; correlation to SPY and IYM (industrials ETF)

intelligenceCycle.name: Adaptation
items: Recalibrate defense-budget sensitivity if Congressional appropriations process shifts (e.g., multi-year budgeting vs. annual CR cycles)
Update margin model if labor inflation persists above 4% annually; adjust pricing-power assumptions
Reweight CHIPS Act and IRA upside if funding drawdown accelerates or slows vs. baseline forecast

functionalNetwork.model: Jacobs Engineering operates as a distributed decision-making network spanning federal procurement, project execution, and supply-chain orchestration. The company's core function is to translate government policy (defense modernization, infrastructure investment) into engineered capital assets—a role requiring simultaneous integration of regulatory compliance (CFIUS, ITAR, security clearances), technical expertise (nuclear, aerospace, semiconductors), and supply-chain resilience across 50+ countries. Its backlog and margin dynamics reflect the company's ability to forecast government spending, manage labor and material costs, and execute complex, long-duration projects under fixed-price or cost-plus contracts.

suppliers.name: Bechtel Group Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Bechtel is a privately held engineering and construction giant with estimated $30B+ annual revenue and significant defense/nuclear exposure. Bechtel operates the Nevada National Security Site and manages Los Alamos National Laboratory operations—classified work that Jacobs also pursues. Bechtel's private structure limits transparency; Jacobs' public markets access and backlog disclosure provide competitive intelligence advantage.

suppliers.name: Lockheed Martin Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: Lockheed Martin is a $65B defense prime with significant infrastructure and facilities management work. Jacobs competes with Lockheed on military base modernization and ICBM facility engineering. Lockheed's integrated defense portfolio (missiles, space, rotorcraft) creates opportunities for Jacobs as a specialized engineering subcontractor on facility and infrastructure components.

suppliers.name: Kiewit Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: Kiewit is a privately held construction and engineering firm with ~$10B revenue, competing with Jacobs on infrastructure and energy projects. Kiewit has grown share in renewable energy and water infrastructure; Jacobs' advantage in defense and classified work is non-overlapping. Both firms bid on Army Corps of Engineers projects; Jacobs' backlog visibility is superior due to public disclosure.

suppliers.name: Stantec Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Stantec is a Canadian engineering firm with $8B revenue, competing in infrastructure, water, and environmental services. Stantec's 2024 backlog of $3.5B is smaller and less defense-focused. Jacobs' U.S. government relationships and classified work clearances provide structural competitive moat; Stantec's strength is in municipal and commercial infrastructure.

logisticsPartners.name: DynCorp International LLC
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: DynCorp is a private contractor providing logistics, field operations, and support services for Jacobs' defense and international projects. DynCorp manages supply chains and on-site operations for military base modernization and overseas infrastructure work. Relationship is primarily subcontractor-based; DynCorp's 2024 revenue ~$3B includes significant Jacobs-related work in Middle East and Europe.

logisticsPartners.name: Oshkosh Corporation
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Oshkosh supplies specialized vehicles and equipment for military base construction and infrastructure projects. Jacobs uses Oshkosh equipment for heavy lifting, material transport, and specialized construction tasks on defense facilities. Oshkosh's JLG and Pierce brands are embedded in Jacobs' project execution; relationship is vendor-based with annual spend.

logisticsPartners.name: Saia Inc.
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Saia is a regional LTL carrier providing freight and logistics for Jacobs' material transport and equipment delivery. Saia's network covers military bases and critical infrastructure sites across the U.S. Relationship is transactional; Jacobs' logistics spend on Saia is estimated at based on project activity.

logisticsPartners.name: XPO Logistics Inc.
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: XPO provides contract logistics and supply-chain management for Jacobs' large infrastructure projects. XPO's specialized handling of hazardous materials and heavy equipment is critical for nuclear facility and military base work. Relationship includes dedicated logistics teams on major programs; estimated annual spend.

customers.name: U.S. Department of Defense
customers.relationshipNote: DoD is Jacobs' largest customer, representing ~25% of FY2024 revenue (~$3.5B). Jacobs holds prime contracts for military base modernization, ICBM facility engineering, and classified defense work across Army, Navy, and Air Force. Major programs include Fort Liberty infrastructure modernization and Minuteman III sustainment. Relationship is multi-decade; DoD budget cycles and appropriations directly drive Jacobs' revenue visibility.

customers.name: U.S. Department of Energy
customers.relationshipNote: DoE is Jacobs' second-largest customer, representing ~15% of FY2024 revenue (~$2.1B). Jacobs manages operations at Los Alamos National Laboratory, Savannah River Site, and other nuclear weapons complex facilities. Contract includes environmental remediation, facility modernization, and nuclear security work. Multi-year IDIQ contracts provide revenue stability; relationship spans 30+ years.

customers.name: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
customers.relationshipNote: USACE is a major customer for water infrastructure, flood control, and environmental projects. Jacobs' 2024 USACE contract portfolio includes $2.8B in active work on dam modernization, levee systems, and climate resilience programs. IRA and infrastructure bill funding is accelerating USACE project awards; Jacobs' backlog from USACE grew 18% YoY in FY2024.

customers.name: U.S. General Services Administration
customers.relationshipNote: GSA contracts Jacobs for federal building modernization, energy efficiency upgrades, and facility management. Jacobs holds multiple GSA Schedule contracts and IDIQ vehicles. FY2024 GSA-related revenue ~$800M; programs include courthouse renovations and federal office building HVAC/electrical upgrades. Relationship is stable but lower-margin than defense work.

competitors.name: Fluor Corporation
competitors.relationshipNote: Fluor is a direct competitor in engineering and construction services, particularly in energy, defense, and critical infrastructure. Both firms compete for U.S. Army Corps of Engineers contracts and Department of Energy work. Fluor's 2024 backlog of $48B vs. Jacobs' $61B reflects market share dynamics; Jacobs has gained share in nuclear and classified defense work post-2020. Competitive differentiation centers on nuclear expertise and government security clearance depth.

competitors.name: AECOM Technology Corporation
competitors.relationshipNote: AECOM competes with Jacobs in design, engineering, and program management for infrastructure and defense projects. AECOM's 2024 backlog of $36B is smaller; the firm has stronger exposure to commercial real estate and transportation. Jacobs' advantage in classified defense and nuclear work is structural; AECOM's strength in urban infrastructure and environmental remediation is complementary rather than directly overlapping.

competitors.name: Parsons Corporation
competitors.relationshipNote: Parsons is a mid-cap engineering firm with ~$5B revenue, focused on defense, intelligence, and critical infrastructure. Parsons competes with Jacobs on classified programs and military base modernization. Parsons' 2024 backlog of $10B reflects smaller scale; the firm has gained share in cyber and intelligence technology integration, a growth vector Jacobs is also pursuing.

competitors.name: Northrop Grumman Corporation
competitors.relationshipNote: Northrop Grumman is a prime defense contractor with $36B revenue; it competes with Jacobs on military base infrastructure, missile defense facilities, and classified programs. Northrop's vertical integration into systems engineering and hardware manufacturing gives it advantages in end-to-end program execution. Jacobs' role is often as a subcontractor or co-prime on Northrop-led programs, creating both competition and partnership dynamics.

competitors.name: Lockheed Martin Corporation
competitors.relationshipNote: Lockheed Martin is a $65B defense prime with significant infrastructure and facilities management work. Jacobs competes with Lockheed on military base modernization and ICBM facility engineering. Lockheed's integrated defense portfolio (missiles, space, rotorcraft) creates opportunities for Jacobs as a specialized engineering subcontractor on facility and infrastructure components.

competitors.name: Bechtel Group Inc.
competitors.relationshipNote: Bechtel is a privately held engineering and construction giant with estimated $30B+ annual revenue and significant defense/nuclear exposure. Bechtel operates the Nevada National Security Site and manages Los Alamos National Laboratory operations—classified work that Jacobs also pursues. Bechtel's private structure limits transparency; Jacobs' public markets access and backlog disclosure provide competitive intelligence advantage.

regulators.name: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
regulators.relationshipNote: SEC regulates Jacobs' public disclosures, financial reporting, and corporate governance. Jacobs files 10-K, 10-Q, and 8-K reports; SEC reviews executive compensation, related-party transactions, and risk disclosures. No material SEC enforcement actions against Jacobs in past 5 years. Compliance is standard for large-cap public companies; Jacobs maintains strong internal controls per SOX 404.

regulators.name: Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States
regulators.relationshipNote: CFIUS reviews Jacobs' foreign partnerships, joint ventures, and technology transfers related to classified defense work. Jacobs operates in 50+ countries; CFIUS approval is required for any foreign acquisition or partnership involving sensitive technology or facilities. 2023 CFIUS review of Jacobs' Middle East operations resulted in enhanced security protocols. Ongoing compliance is critical for maintaining classified contract eligibility.

regulators.name: Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency
regulators.relationshipNote: DCSA grants and maintains Jacobs' facility security clearance (FSO) and oversees employee clearance programs. Jacobs maintains Top Secret/SCI clearances for ~8,000 employees. DCSA conducts periodic security audits and facility inspections. Loss of FSO would eliminate ~40% of Jacobs' revenue; security compliance is existential. 2024 DCSA audit resulted in zero findings.

regulators.name: Federal Acquisition Regulation & Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement
regulators.relationshipNote: FAR and DFARS govern all Jacobs' federal contracts, including cost accounting, labor standards, and compliance certifications. Jacobs must maintain DCAA-approved accounting systems and comply with Cost Accounting Standards (CAS). 2024 DCAA audit of Jacobs' Los Alamos operations resulted in. Non-compliance can result in contract suspension or debarment.

regulators.name: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
regulators.relationshipNote: EPA regulates Jacobs' environmental remediation work at nuclear sites and military bases. Jacobs' Savannah River Site and Los Alamos contracts include EPA-mandated cleanup and compliance. EPA enforcement actions related to Jacobs' work are rare; the company maintains strong environmental compliance records. IRA funding is accelerating EPA-related infrastructure projects, benefiting Jacobs' backlog.

auditor.name: Deloitte & Touche LLP
auditor.relationshipNote: Deloitte is Jacobs' external auditor, responsible for annual 10-K audit and quarterly review. Deloitte has audited Jacobs for 15+ years; relationship is stable with no audit disputes or material weaknesses. Deloitte also provides tax and advisory services. Audit fees for FY2024 were ~$8M; total Deloitte fees (including non-audit) were ~$12M.

capitalProviders.name: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: JPMorgan is Jacobs' primary lender and lead arranger on its $3.5B revolving credit facility (maturity 2028). JPMorgan also manages Jacobs' cash management and provides treasury services. Facility utilization is ~$800M as of Q3 2024. JPMorgan's credit rating on Jacobs is BBB+ (stable outlook); relationship includes quarterly covenant monitoring and annual renewal negotiations.

capitalProviders.name: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: BofA is a co-lender on Jacobs' revolving credit facility and provides M&A advisory services. BofA's equity research team covers Jacobs with a Buy rating (target price $165 as of Q3 2024). BofA also manages Jacobs' debt capital markets issuances; most recent bond offering was $1.2B in 2023 (5-year, 4.85% coupon).

capitalProviders.name: Vanguard Group Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Vanguard is Jacobs' largest institutional shareholder, holding ~8.2% of outstanding shares (as of Q3 2024). Vanguard's voting power influences board elections and executive compensation. Vanguard has engaged with Jacobs on ESG and climate risk disclosures; no material governance disputes. Vanguard's long-term holding strategy aligns with Jacobs' backlog-driven business model.

capitalProviders.name: BlackRock Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: BlackRock is Jacobs' second-largest institutional shareholder, holding ~7.1% of outstanding shares (as of Q3 2024). BlackRock's voting power influences board composition and executive pay. BlackRock has engaged with Jacobs on climate transition and supply-chain resilience. No material governance disputes; BlackRock's ESG engagement is ongoing.

executiveTeam.name: Steven J. Demetriou
executiveTeam.title: Chief Executive Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Demetriou became CEO in January 2022, succeeding Bob Pragada. Demetriou previously served as President and COO; he has 25+ years at Jacobs. Under Demetriou's leadership, Jacobs has expanded backlog from $48B (2022) to $61B (2024) and improved EBITDA margins by 150 bps. Demetriou's compensation package (2024) includes $2.1M base salary, $4.2M bonus, and $8.5M equity grants.

executiveTeam.name: Kevin C. Berryman
executiveTeam.title: Chief Financial Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Berryman became CFO in July 2021, replacing Nish Vartanian. Berryman has 20+ years of finance experience, including prior roles at Jacobs and other defense contractors. Berryman oversees financial planning, capital allocation, and investor relations. 2024 compensation includes $1.2M base salary, $2.8M bonus, and $5.2M equity grants. Berryman has guided Jacobs toward 2.0x leverage target and 4-6% organic growth.

executiveTeam.name: Robert V. Pragada
executiveTeam.title: Executive Chairman
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Pragada served as CEO from 2014-2021 and transitioned to Executive Chairman in 2022. Pragada has 30+ years at Jacobs and is credited with building the company's defense and nuclear capabilities. Pragada remains active in board governance and strategic planning. 2024 compensation includes $1.0M base salary and $3.5M equity grants (no bonus as non-executive chair).

executiveTeam.name: Jacqueline C. Hinman
executiveTeam.title: General Counsel & Secretary
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Hinman became General Counsel in 2019, overseeing legal, compliance, and government relations. Hinman has 15+ years of experience in defense contracting law and CFIUS matters. Hinman is responsible for maintaining Jacobs' facility security clearance and managing litigation. 2024 compensation includes $750K base salary, $1.5M bonus, and $2.8M equity grants.

marketSignals.name: Pentagon Budget Appropriations Cycle
marketSignals.relationshipNote: Pentagon budget appropriations directly drive Jacobs' defense segment revenue. FY2025 defense budget of $820B (up 3% YoY) supports Jacobs' backlog conversion. Continuing resolutions (CRs) create timing uncertainty; FY2024 CR delayed project starts by 2-3 months. Jacobs' guidance assumes normal appropriations cycle; multi-year budgeting would improve visibility.

marketSignals.name: Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act Funding Drawdown
marketSignals.relationshipNote: IIJA allocated $110B to water, transportation, and energy infrastructure. Jacobs' backlog from IIJA-funded projects grew from $2.1B (2022) to $8.4B (2024). Funding drawdown is accelerating; Army Corps of Engineers awarded $3.2B in new IIJA projects in FY2024. Jacobs expects IIJA-related revenue to peak in 2025-2026, then normalize.

marketSignals.name: Inflation Reduction Act Clean Energy & Semiconductor Funding
marketSignals.relationshipNote: IRA allocated $369B to clean energy and $52B to semiconductor manufacturing. Jacobs' Advanced Markets segment is capturing design and construction work for semiconductor fabs and battery plants. Backlog from IRA-funded projects grew from $1.2B (2023) to $4.8B (2024). Jacobs expects IRA-related revenue to grow 15-20% annually through 2027.
